summary: This benchmark investigates the causal portability of an isolated attention head in a synthetic 16-register memory routing task. By transplanting a 98,304-weight head from an intact donor into an adapted host and evaluating both addition and removal controls, the study demonstrates that while individual answer recalls transfer causally, broader donor performance fails to transfer (achieving only a 3.23-point gain versus the preregistered 5-point threshold). The methodology and statistical reporting are thorough and transparent, though bounded by the synthetic nature of the task.
strengths: Rigorous experimental controls, including an adapted host baseline, a donor head graft, and a restored native head ablation to distinguish donor-driven solves from noise.
Precise statistical reporting with paired 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for both transfer gain and donor removal degradation.
Transparent reporting of negative results against preregistered criteria (failing to meet the 5-point transfer bar).
Flawless architectural and parameter accounting, where head dimension (98,304 weights) and downstream block parameters (1,770,240 weights) match standard transformer specifications.
weaknesses: Evaluated purely on a narrow 16-register synthetic task with an artificial attention mask displacement, limiting external validity to natural language models and real-world transfer learning.
Restricted to a single model scale (8 blocks, width 384) descended from a single shared initialization seed.
Explores only a single-head transplant at block 4 rather than benchmarking multiple heads, different layer depths, or multi-head ensembles.
suggestions: Extend the benchmark to evaluate head transplantability across different transformer layers to determine if lower- or higher-level heads exhibit distinct transfer dynamics.
Test whether transferring multi-head circuits or full attention sublayers closes the performance gap toward the intact donor.
Evaluate whether similar localized transfer phenomena hold in standard NLP benchmark tasks (e.g., indirect object identification or factual recall).

claims.text: Model stitching has previously examined compatibility of neural representations using learned connections. [Bansal and colleagues, NeurIPS 2021]
A 98,304-weight attention-head transplant made a weak transformer solve 831 register-memory queries its matched host missed.
claims.source: Mathematical verification: For width 384 and head dimension 64, Q, K, V, and O projections yield 4 * 384 * 64 = 98,304 parameters.

claims.text: Each trained just the following block, 1,770,240 weights, for 1,024 updates on the same fresh program batches.
claims.source: Mathematical verification: A width-384 transformer block with 4x MLP expansion comprises 4 * 384^2 (attention) + 8 * 384^2 (MLP) + 2 * 384 (LayerNorms) = 1,770,240 parameters.

claims.text: Balanced accuracy increased from 10.45% to 13.68%, below the preregistered five-point transfer threshold and far below the intact donor’s 92.08%.
claims.source: Table 1 arithmetic check: 13.68% - 10.45% = 3.23 percentage points, consistent with the reported 3.23-point gain.

novelty_vs_existing.title: Revisiting Model Stitching to Compare Neural Representations (Bansal et al., NeurIPS 2021)
novelty_vs_existing.contribution: Whereas Bansal et al. used trainable stitching layers between frozen model halves to assess representational compatibility, this benchmark tests direct transplant of a single functional attention head with donor-off ablation controls on a discrete register-tracking task.
